html_source:
In brief

Parody. "A large and appreciative gathering of friends and acquaintances [...] Visszontlátásra, kedvès baráton! Visszontlátásra! Gone but not forgotten": as Bloom departs on the castle car with the Citizen hurling antisemitic abuse and onlookers jeering in the street, he in turn shouting defiant pride in his Jewishness, a long paragraph describes the leavetaking as a lovefest between the Irish people and a royal Hungarian visitor. A dig at Queen Victoria's rapturous 1900 reception in Dublin is implicit. This irruption continues the nautical conceit of the previous one—though here the ship is floating down the Liffey rather than setting sail—and it adopts the overblown style of contemporary newspapers, as in several earlier parodies.

At more length

Gifford plausibly suggests that this passage "Parodies a newspaper account of the departure of a royal foreign visitor." Several details create the impression of royalty. A crowd of wellwishers gathers to bid farewell to "Nagyaságos uram Lipóti Virag." The Hungarian word order is wrong, but the archaic deferential phrase nagyaságos uram means "my lord," "your excellency," or "great sir." The flags "dipped in salute" along the Liffey would be appropriate to a head of state, and Slote, Mamigonian, and Turner note that the two gifts presented to the great man—"An illuminated scroll of ancient Irish vellum" and "a silver casket, tastefully executed in the style of ancient Celtic ornament"—precisely recall "the freedom casket presented to Queen Victoria by the Corporation on her visit to Dublin" in April 1900. They quote from Michael McCarthy's Five Years in Ireland (1901): "The Town Clerk then read the address, which was enclosed in a golden casket of ancient Celtic design, and rested on a cushion of green silk, trimmed with gold border and tassels" (478).

The subversive implications of painting Bloom as a revered foreign monarch become clear when one realizes that the "silver casket" presented to him by his Irish admirers, having been made by "Messrs Jacob agus Jacob" (agus is Irish for "and"), is a mocking name for the Jacob's "biscuitbox" which the Citizen is reaching for to "murder him." In 1900 the civic authorities of Dublin presented a gold box to their Queen as part of a royal visit that drew huge appreciative crowds. In Cyclops appreciative crowds look on as a silver one is dispatched toward a foreign visitor with more overtly hostile intent. Victoria returned to England on the Royal Yacht, and Bloom too departs on his "pleasureship."

The cyclopean exaggerations in this parody recall those in the execution scene. Thousands of people gather to cheer the noble man. Celebratory fires are lit on mountains and coastlines throughout Ireland (the "four seas" are the Irish Sea, the Atlantic Ocean, the North Channel, and the St. George's Channel), and Ireland's cheers are met "by answering cheers from a big muster of henchmen on the distant Cambrian and Caledonian hills" in Wales and Scotland. The "mastodontic" ship carrying the monarch—unimaginably large, in galumphing journalistic hyperbole—is paid "a final floral tribute" by women casting bouquets of flowers onto the water from the quays, and "a flotilla of barges" escorts the ship out of town.

Only one detail performs the kind of bathetic, sarcastic puncturing encountered repeatedly in the execution parody. Bloom is said to be bound for "the distant clime of Százharminczbrojúgulyas-Dugulas (Meadow of Murmuring Waters)." Slote cites Tekla Meksnóber's observation in "'Inbursts of maggyer': Joyce, the Fall, and the Magyar Language," Hungarian Studies 26 (June 2012), that this long compound translates not to Meadow of Murmuring Waters but to "blockage caused by 130 portions of veal goulash" (98). Joyce evidently could not resist adding a crude joke about gluttony and constipation to the tissue of false compliments. A final scrap of Hungarian, "Visszontlátásra, kedvès baráton! Visszontlátásra!," is more benign. It means "See you again, my dear friend! See you again!" 

John Hunt 2026
